blocks.text: **The problem.** Design the history of one browser tab. `BrowserHistory(homepage)` starts on the homepage. `visit(url)` goes to a new page and **clears all forward history**. `back(steps)` moves back up to `steps` pages and `forward(steps)` forward up to `steps` pages — stopping early if history runs out — and both return the page you end up on.

blocks.alt: Browser history as a doubly linked list of pages: home, news, mail, maps. The current page is mail. Back follows the prev arrows to news and home; forward follows the next arrow to maps. Visiting a new page from mail would replace maps: the forward history is dropped.

blocks.text: The idea: history is a line you move along in both directions

Pages form a sequence with a **current position**. Back moves one way, forward the other, and a visit **cuts off** everything ahead of the current page before adding the new one. A doubly linked list models this exactly: each page node has `prev` (where back goes) and `next` (where forward goes). Visiting is: link a new node after the current one — setting `curr.next` to it is what drops the old forward pages.
Keep the pages behind you on a **back stack** and the pages ahead on a **forward stack**. Going back moves the current page onto the forward stack; visiting clears the forward stack.

**Visit O(1)** (clearing a stack can cost its size, but each page is cleared at most once), **back and forward O(steps)**, **space O(n)** for n visited pages. Every move copies a page from one stack to the other.

blocks.caption: Each page is a node; back follows prev, forward follows next, and visit cuts off what was ahead.

blocks.text: **Visit O(1), back and forward O(steps), space O(n).** Nothing is copied: moving is just following an arrow, and dropping the forward history is a single pointer change. (In C++, the dropped pages should also be freed; garbage-collected languages reclaim them automatically.)
3. Array with a current index and an end marker

Keep the pages in an array, an index `curr` for the page on screen, and `last`, the furthest index forward is allowed to reach. Visiting writes at `curr + 1` and sets `last` there — older pages beyond it are simply ignored. Back and forward become arithmetic.
**Every operation O(1)** (visit amortized, for the array growing), **space O(n).** Being able to jump `steps` positions at once is the one thing an array does better than a linked list.

blocks.alt: Two stacks: O(steps) time, O(n) space. Doubly linked list: O(steps) time, O(n) space. Array + index: O(1) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: The doubly linked list is the natural model — it's how most people picture history — and it's what interviewers want to hear first. Then show the array version: once you notice that **only the current position and the end** matter, back and forward become O(1).

items: **Back past the homepage** — `back(7)` with three pages behind you stops at the homepage.
**Forward with nothing ahead** — returns the current page.
**Visit after going back** — the old forward pages must be gone: `forward` can't reach them.
**Visiting the same page twice** — it's a new entry each time, not a jump to the old one.
**LRU Cache** — another design question built on a doubly linked list, this time with a hash map. Two lessons on.
**Undo / redo** — the same structure: undo is back, redo is forward, and a new edit clears the redo history.
**Design a Text Editor** — a cursor in a doubly linked list of characters (or two stacks), moving left and right.
